parsed_answer.content:
Native Images, spearheaded by the GraalVM project, represent a revolutionary paradigm shift in how Java and Spring applications are compiled, packaged, and executed. Traditionally, Java applications run on a Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler within the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). Bytecode is loaded dynamically, analyzed at runtime, and optimized on the fly as hotspots are identified. While this provides phenomenal peak performance and runtime adaptability, it comes with heavy memory footprints and protracted startup times. Spring Native, which has now evolved directly into Spring Boot 3's core AOT (Ahead-Of-Time) processing engine, bridges the gap between the classic Java ecosystem and the world of lightning-fast standalone binaries. 

By leveraging GraalVM's substrate VM, Native Images compile Java bytecode directly into a machine-code executable ahead of time. This process completely eliminates the JVM startup phase, dropping cold-start latency from seconds or minutes down to mere milliseconds, while drastically lowering the resident set size (RSS) memory consumption. However, this transformation requires a radical departure from traditional Java dynamics. Because Native Images utilize a Closed-World Assumption—meaning all classes, methods, and fields must be known at compile-time—dynamic features like runtime reflection, dynamic proxies, Resource loading, and dependency injection via dynamic class loading break unless explicitly declared or processed ahead of time. The Spring AOT engine inspects your application context during build time, generating the necessary configuration hints (such as reflection and serialization configuration JSONs) so that the GraalVM native-image compiler can build a fully functioning standalone binary without runtime surprises.

rows: Seconds to minutes (Class loading, JIT warming)
Higher baseline (Metaspace, JIT compiler threads, GC overhead)
Significantly smaller (No JVM runtime, minimal heap overhead)
Very slow (Requires heavy AOT analysis and whole-program optimization)
Full support for runtime reflection, proxies, and dynamic class loading
Constrained by Closed-World Assumption; requires explicit configuration hints

items: The Closed-World Assumption dictates that everything not explicitly reachable from the application's entry points during static analysis is stripped away by dead-code elimination (DCE).
Spring Boot 3's AOT engine intercepts the application bootstrap phase, executing the BeanFactory initialization at build time to generate static configuration and remove runtime container overhead.
Reflection, JNI, Resource bundles, and Proxies require explicit metadata registration via Reachability Metadata files or programmatic Hints provided by framework starters.
Garbage collection in native images defaults to Serial GC (or epsilon/g1 in enterprise editions), changing latency and throughput profiles compared to G1 or ZGC on the traditional JVM.

parsed_answer.content: When migrating large enterprise Spring applications to Native Images, watch out for third-party libraries that rely heavily on un-annotated reflection or dynamic class scanning (e.g., legacy database drivers, old object mappers, or custom plugin architectures). If a library fails to supply GraalVM reachability metadata, your native binary will compile successfully but throw catastrophic ClassNotFoundException or NoSuchMethodException errors at runtime when that specific code path is first evaluated. Always run comprehensive integration tests against the actual built native executable using Maven/Gradle native test plugins before pushing to production.
